headline: VFW and 25 other veterans groups ask Congress to regulate hemp, not ban it
dek: A 17 November letter from 26 veterans groups and veteran-owned firms urges congressional leaders to replace the 11 December hemp THC ban with age limits, testing and labels.
key_points: Twenty-six veterans organisations and veteran-owned businesses, including the VFW, wrote to congressional leaders on 17 November 2026.
They ask Congress to swap the 11 December hemp THC restrictions for a federal framework: 21+ sales, age checks, lab testing, labels and serving limits.
West Virginia's agriculture commissioner, Kent Leonhardt, made a similar case days earlier, pointing to his state's registration system.
Rep. James Comer has said a must-pass spending bill is the best vehicle for any fix before the deadline.
body: A coalition of 26 veterans organisations and veteran-owned businesses, led by the Veterans of Foreign Wars, asked Congress on 17 November to regulate hemp-derived THC rather than let a near-total ban take effect on 11 December. The letter went to House Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Democratic leaders Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, and senior appropriators in both chambers, according to The Marijuana Herald, which published details of the letter.

The group's core message is short: regulate hemp, do not eliminate it. The signatories accept that Congress has real concerns about sales to minors and weak oversight, but argue that a blanket ban fixes neither and pushes buyers to sellers who do no testing and check no IDs.
## What the veterans are asking for

The coalition proposes a federal framework in place of the ban. Every buyer of hemp THC products would have to be 21 or older, with real age verification at the point of sale. Products would need third-party lab testing, accurate labels, child-resistant packaging and set limits on serving size. Manufacturers and retailers would work under defined federal oversight, and businesses that comply would be protected.

Signatories include the VFW, the Non Commissioned Officers Association, National American Indian Veterans, Burn Pits 360, Grunt Style Foundation, Irreverent Warriors, Operation Green Healing and Veteran Initiative 22, plus individual VFW posts in Missouri and Texas and several veteran-owned hemp firms. The letter says the signers support the recommendations independently and were not paid.

The groups put weight on veterans who use hemp products for chronic pain, post-traumatic stress, anxiety and sleep, some of them alongside their doctors as an alternative to opioids. They also warn that the ban would close compliant businesses that veterans own or staff. MetaFlora News is reporting the groups' stated reasons, not endorsing any health claim.
> The hemp fight is no longer farmers against police. When the VFW signs on, the politics of a December ban get harder for both parties.
## A Republican regulator says the same

The letter follows an op-ed from West Virginia Agriculture Commissioner Kent Leonhardt, a Republican, published on 13 November. He urged Congress to stop the ban and copy his state's approach. West Virginia requires manufacturers and retailers of hemp-derived products to register with its agriculture department, tests products for potency and contaminants, and limits intoxicating hemp sales to people 21 and over.

According to department figures from May 2024 cited by The Marijuana Herald, the state then had 1,063 registered hemp retailers and 1,707 registered products, and inspectors had carried out 276 inspections in 45 counties and seized 611 illegal products.

The restrictions come from the law President Trump signed in November 2025, which narrowed the federal definition of hemp to exclude finished products with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. That would remove most intoxicating hemp products and many non-intoxicating CBD products with trace THC. Congress later pushed most of the change from 12 November to 11 December 2026 through a stopgap spending bill that funds federal agencies to that same date, Filter reported, which is why the hemp deadline and the next funding deadline now fall on one day. The part that excludes certain synthetic cannabinoids took effect on 12 November, as we reported that day.

Time is short. As we reported on 16 November, Rep. James Comer of Kentucky said attaching hemp language to must-pass spending legislation is the industry's best chance before the deadline. As we reported on 14 November, senators remain split: Nebraska Republican Pete Ricketts wants no further delay, while Minnesota Democrat Amy Klobuchar wants a fix.

Big retailers are also pushing. The Marijuana Herald reported on 4 November that Total Wine & More had registered a new outside lobbying firm on hemp beverages and spent $510,000 on lobbying in the first nine months of 2026, backing the Beverage Regulatory Parity Act (H.R. 10079), which would allow drinks with up to 5 milligrams of THC per serving under alcohol-style rules.

Watch the text of the next government funding bill and whether it carries any hemp language or a further delay. Watch whether more traditional veterans groups, such as the American Legion, add their names. And watch 11 December: without action, retailers in states that have not set their own rules face the biggest overnight change.
